AlphaCom Customer Churn: Interim Notebook

Companion notebook to the interim project report. It covers the four interim sections:

  1. Understanding the business problem
  2. Exploratory data analysis
  3. Data preprocessing
  4. Model building: baseline model

Every figure used in the report is produced here and saved into a figures/ folder. Run the cells from top to bottom; customer_churn.csv must sit in the same folder as the notebook.

1. Understanding the Business Problem

AlphaCom is a telecom provider whose customer churn has been rising even though its prices and product range are competitive. Existing retention campaigns are broad and reactive, so money is spent on customers who were never going to leave and the ones who do leave are noticed too late.

Objective. Build a model that scores each customer on the likelihood of leaving, and find out which customer and service characteristics push that likelihood up or down. The output should let the retention team contact the right customers early, with an offer that fits the reason they are likely to leave.

Target variable. Churn (Yes = the customer left).

Why it matters. Winning a new customer costs more than keeping an existing one, and a churned subscriber takes every future month of revenue with them. A model that finds even a modest share of the future leavers in advance protects revenue directly.

2.2 Data overview

Before any plotting, the raw file is scanned for problems. info() already shows that MonthlyCharges and TotalCharges were read as text, and tenure has missing values.

def money_literal(s, lit):
    return s.astype(str).str.strip().str.lower().eq(lit).sum()

issue_log = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Churn written in different forms (case / spaces)", "Churn", raw["Churn"].nunique(), "Standardise to Yes / No"),

In [6]:
PAY_MAP = {"electronic check": "Electronic check", "mailed check": "Mailed check",
           "bank transfer (automatic)": "Bank transfer (auto)", "credit card (automatic)": "Credit card (auto)"}

def standardise(frame):
    """Fix labels and data types. Row-wise only, nothing is learned from the data."""
    d = frame.copy()
    text_cols = [c for c in d.columns if c not in ("tenure", "SeniorCitizen", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges")]
    for c in text_cols:
        d[c] = d[c].astype(str).str.strip()
    d["PaymentMethod"] = d["PaymentMethod"].str.lower().map(PAY_MAP)
    d["Churn"] = d["Churn"].str.lower().map({"yes": "Yes", "no": "No"})
    for c in ("MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"):
        d[c] = pd.to_numeric(d[c].astype(str).str.replace(r"[^0-9.\-]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
    return d

eda = standardise(raw)
eda.loc[eda["tenure"] < 0, "tenure"] = np.nan          # impossible
eda.loc[eda["TotalCharges"] < 0, "TotalCharges"] = np.nan   # impossible
eda.dtypes.to_frame("dtype").T

def count_grid(cols, ncols, name, figsize, wrap_w=10):
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(cols) / ncols))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=figsize)
    axes = np.array(axes).ravel()
    for i, col in enumerate(cols):
        vc = eda[col].value_counts()
        pct = vc / vc.sum() * 100
        cols_i = [CYCLE[j % len(CYCLE)] for j in range(len(vc))]
        axes[i].bar(wrap([str(x) for x in vc.index], wrap_w), vc.values, color=cols_i, width=0.65)
        for j, (v, p) in enumerate(zip(vc.values, pct)):
            axes[i].text(j, v + vc.max() * 0.02, f"{p:.2f}%", ha="center", fontsize=9.5)
        axes[i].set_ylim(0, vc.max() * 1.15)
        axes[i].set_title(col)
        axes[i].tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=9.5)
        axes[i].set_ylabel("Customers" if i % ncols == 0 else "")
    for k in range(len(cols), len(axes)):
        axes[k].axis("off")
    plt.tight_layout()
    save(name)
    plt.show()

eda["ChurnFlag"] = (eda["Churn"] == "Yes").astype(int)
overall = eda["ChurnFlag"].mean() * 100

def rate_grid(cols, ncols, name, figsize, wrap_w=10):
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(cols) / ncols))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=figsize)
    axes = np.array(axes).ravel()
    for i, col in enumerate(cols):
        r = eda.groupby(col)["ChurnFlag"].mean().mul(100).sort_values(ascending=False)
        pal = [C["churn"] if v > overall * 1.05 else (C["stay"] if v < overall * 0.95 else C["grey"]) for v in r.values]
        axes[i].bar(wrap([str(x) for x in r.index], wrap_w), r.values, color=pal, width=0.65)
        axes[i].axhline(overall, color=C["navy"], ls="--", lw=1.4)
        for j, v in enumerate(r.values):
            axes[i].text(j, v + 1, f"{v:.2f}%", ha="center", fontsize=9.5)
        axes[i].set_ylim(0, max(r.max() * 1.18, overall * 1.3))
        axes[i].set_title(col)
        axes[i].tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=9.5)
        axes[i].set_ylabel("Churn rate (%)" if i % ncols == 0 else "")
    for k in range(len(cols), len(axes)):
        axes[k].axis("off")
    plt.tight_layout()
    save(name)
    plt.show()

Statistical check. A chi-square test of independence between each categorical variable and churn, with Cramér's V as the strength of the association (0 = none, 1 = perfect). With 12,000 rows nearly everything is "significant", so the effect size is what ranks the variables.

In [15]:
rows = []
for col in cat_cols:
    ct = pd.crosstab(eda[col], eda["Churn"])
    chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
    v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (ct.values.sum() * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
    rows.append((col, chi2, p, v))
assoc = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Variable", "Chi-square", "p-value", "Cramer's V"]).sort_values("Cramer's V", ascending=False)
assoc["Strength"] = pd.cut(assoc["Cramer's V"], [-1, 0.05, 0.15, 0.3, 1], labels=["Negligible", "Weak", "Moderate", "Strong"])
assoc = assoc.reset_index(drop=True)
assoc["p-value"] = assoc["p-value"].map(lambda x: "<0.0001" if x < 0.0001 else f"{x:.4f}")
assoc

2.6 Observations from the EDA

  • About 28% of customers churned (3,405 of 12,055 before duplicates are removed).
  • Contract is the strongest single signal: month-to-month 46%, one year 11%, two year 3%. Cramér's V = 0.44.
  • Tenure: churn is 48% in the first year and falls to under 10% after four years. Churners have a median tenure of 9 months against 38 for stayers.
  • Internet service: fiber optic 45%, DSL 22%, no internet 9%.
  • Payment method: electronic check 49%; automatic bank transfer or credit card 14 to 16%.
  • Add-ons: customers without tech support or online security churn at roughly three times the rate of those with them. Part of this effect comes from the "No internet service" level.
  • Bills: churners pay more per month on average ($73 against $61).
  • Gender and the phone columns show practically no link with churn.
  • Combinations matter: month-to-month on fiber optic churns at 59%, a two-year customer with no internet at under 3%.

3. Data Preprocessing

The checks follow the order used in the report. Anything that learns from the data (imputation, scaling) is fitted on the training set only, so the train-test split is made before those steps.

Decision. Impossible values were blanked (above). The large gaps between reported and expected totals sit mostly in the later part of the file, which looks like data merged from a second source. Because the cause cannot be identified from the data alone, the reported totals are kept, and Section 3.11 tests whether correcting or dropping them changes the model.

3.6 Missing value treatment

Step 1: encode the categorical columns so that an imputer can use them as clues. "No internet service" and "No phone service" are folded into "No" for the add-on columns, because InternetService and PhoneService already carry that information.

In [37]:
BINARY = ["Partner", "Dependents", "PhoneService", "PaperlessBilling"]
ADDONS = ["OnlineSecurity", "OnlineBackup", "DeviceProtection", "TechSupport", "StreamingTV", "StreamingMovies"]

def encode(frame):
    d = frame.copy()
    d["gender"] = (d["gender"] == "Male").astype(int)
    for c in BINARY + ADDONS + ["MultipleLines"]:
        d[c] = (d[c] == "Yes").astype(int)
    d = pd.get_dummies(d, columns=["InternetService", "Contract", "PaymentMethod"], dtype=int)
    # reference groups: no internet, month-to-month, electronic check
    return d.drop(columns=["InternetService_No", "Contract_Month-to-month", "PaymentMethod_Electronic check"])

Xtr_enc, Xte_enc = encode(X_train), encode(X_test)
print(Xtr_enc.shape, Xte_enc.shape)
list(Xtr_enc.columns)

(9622, 23) (2406, 23)
Out[37]:
['gender', 'SeniorCitizen', 'Partner', 'Dependents', 'tenure', 'PhoneService', 'MultipleLines', 'OnlineSecurity', 'OnlineBackup', 'DeviceProtection', 'TechSupport', 'StreamingTV', 'StreamingMovies', 'PaperlessBilling', 'MonthlyCharges', 'TotalCharges', 'InternetService_DSL', 'InternetService_Fiber optic', 'Contract_One year', 'Contract_Two year', 'PaymentMethod_Bank transfer (auto)', 'PaymentMethod_Credit card (auto)', 'PaymentMethod_Mailed check']

Step 2: choose the imputation method on evidence. Known values in the training set are hidden at random, each method tries to recover them, and the average error is compared.

In [38]:
def rf_imputer():
    return IterativeImputer(estimator=RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=60, max_depth=8, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED),
                            max_iter=3, random_state=SEED)

rng = np.random.RandomState(SEED)
complete_idx = Xtr_enc.dropna().index
group_col = {"tenure": "Contract", "MonthlyCharges": "InternetService", "TotalCharges": "Contract"}
results = {}

for col in ["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"]:
    hide = rng.choice(complete_idx, 500, replace=False)
    truth = Xtr_enc.loc[hide, col]
    masked = Xtr_enc.copy()
    masked.loc[hide, col] = np.nan
    guess = {}
    guess["Global median"] = pd.Series(masked[col].median(), index=hide)
    grp = X_train[group_col[col]]
    guess["Median by " + group_col[col]] = grp.loc[hide].map(masked[col].groupby(grp).median())
    t, m, tc = masked["tenure"], masked["MonthlyCharges"], masked["TotalCharges"]
    ident = {"tenure": tc / m, "MonthlyCharges": tc / t.replace(0, np.nan), "TotalCharges": t * m}[col]
    guess["Billing identity"] = ident.loc[hide].replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    ii = IterativeImputer(estimator=BayesianRidge(), max_iter=5, random_state=SEED)
    guess["Iterative (linear)"] = pd.DataFrame(ii.fit_transform(masked), columns=masked.columns, index=masked.index).loc[hide, col]
    guess["Iterative (random forest)"] = pd.DataFrame(rf_imputer().fit_transform(masked), columns=masked.columns,
                                                      index=masked.index).loc[hide, col]
    results[col] = {k: (v - truth).abs().mean() for k, v in guess.items()}

def method_name(k):
    return "Median by group" if k.startswith("Median by") else k

imp_table = pd.DataFrame({c: {method_name(k): v for k, v in r.items()} for c, r in results.items()})
imp_table.index.name = "Method"
imp_table

The random-forest iterative imputer is best for tenure and MonthlyCharges. For TotalCharges the simple rule tenure x MonthlyCharges is best. The final treatment therefore uses both. Step 3: fit on the training set and apply to both sets.

In [40]:
imputer = rf_imputer().fit(Xtr_enc)
limits = {"tenure": (0, Xtr_enc["tenure"].max()),
          "MonthlyCharges": (Xtr_enc["MonthlyCharges"].min(), Xtr_enc["MonthlyCharges"].max())}

def impute(enc):
    out = pd.DataFrame(imputer.transform(enc), columns=enc.columns, index=enc.index)
    out["tenure"] = out["tenure"].round().clip(*limits["tenure"])
    out["MonthlyCharges"] = out["MonthlyCharges"].clip(*limits["MonthlyCharges"])
    tc_missing = enc["TotalCharges"].isna()
    out.loc[tc_missing, "TotalCharges"] = out.loc[tc_missing, "tenure"] * out.loc[tc_missing, "MonthlyCharges"]
    return out

Xtr_imp, Xte_imp = impute(Xtr_enc), impute(Xte_enc)
after = pd.DataFrame({"Missing before (train)": Xtr_enc.isna().sum()[["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"]],
                      "Missing after (train)": Xtr_imp.isna().sum()[["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"]],
                      "Missing before (test)": Xte_enc.isna().sum()[["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"]],
                      "Missing after (test)": Xte_imp.isna().sum()[["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"]]})

3.7 Outlier check and treatment

The Tukey (IQR) rule is applied to the observed values: anything beyond 1.5 times the interquartile range from the quartiles is flagged.

In [42]:
rows = []
for col in ["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"]:
    s = df[col].dropna()
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    z = ((s - s.mean()) / s.std()).abs()
    rows.append((col, q1, q3, lo, hi, s.min(), s.max(), ((s < lo) | (s > hi)).sum(), (z > 3).sum()))
outliers = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Variable", "Q1", "Q3", "Lower fence", "Upper fence", "Min", "Max",
                                       "Outside IQR fences", "|z| > 3"])
outliers

3.8 Feature engineering

Four candidate features are built from existing columns and tested by 5-fold cross-validation on the training set, with scaling done inside each fold. Logistic regression is used for the test since that is the baseline model.

In [44]:
def add_features(d):
    d = d.copy()
    d["log_tenure"] = np.log1p(d["tenure"])
    d["NumAddons"] = d[ADDONS].sum(axis=1)
    d["AutoPay"] = d["PaymentMethod_Bank transfer (auto)"] + d["PaymentMethod_Credit card (auto)"]
    d["HasFamily"] = ((d["Partner"] + d["Dependents"]) > 0).astype(int)
    return d

Ftr, Fte = add_features(Xtr_imp), add_features(Xte_imp)
SCALE_CANDIDATES = ["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges", "log_tenure"]

def cv_score(cols):
    scale_cols = [c for c in cols if c in SCALE_CANDIDATES]
    pipe = make_pipeline(ColumnTransformer([("sc", StandardScaler(), scale_cols)], remainder="passthrough"),
                         LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=3000))
    cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
    r = cross_validate(pipe, Ftr[cols], y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["recall", "f1", "roc_auc"])
    return {"Recall": r["test_recall"].mean(), "F1": r["test_f1"].mean(), "ROC-AUC": r["test_roc_auc"].mean()}

base_cols = list(Xtr_imp.columns)
variants = {
    "A. Original encoded columns": base_cols,
    "B. A + log(tenure)": base_cols + ["log_tenure"],
    "C. A with tenure replaced by log(tenure)": [c for c in base_cols if c != "tenure"] + ["log_tenure"],
    "D. A + AutoPay + HasFamily": base_cols + ["AutoPay", "HasFamily"],
    "E. A with six add-ons replaced by their count": [c for c in base_cols if c not in ADDONS] + ["NumAddons"],
}
fe_table = pd.DataFrame({k: cv_score(v) for k, v in variants.items()}).T
fe_table.map(lambda v: f"{v:.4f}")      # four decimals: the differences are small

Adding the logarithm of tenure (variant B) or using it in place of tenure (variant C) gives the best ROC-AUC, 0.8526 against 0.8493 for the original columns, because churn drops fast over the first months and then flattens, which a straight line in tenure cannot follow. B and C are practically tied, so C is used: it has one column fewer and avoids carrying tenure twice. The other ideas add nothing for a linear model (they only repeat information already in the columns), and the add-on count is slightly worse because it hides which add-on matters. NumAddons, AutoPay and HasFamily are kept in the prepared data for the tree-based models of the later stage, but are not used in the baseline.

Churners are about 28% of the data (roughly 1 in 3.5 customers). That is imbalanced enough that a model can look accurate by favouring "stayed", but not so extreme that synthetic samples are needed. The classes are therefore handled with class weights (each churner counts about 2.5 times as much in the loss), which adds no artificial customers and leaves the test set untouched. Both splits are stratified.

Logistic regression is sensitive to the scale of its inputs, so the three continuous columns are standardised. The scaler is fitted on the training set only.

3.11 Multicollinearity check and sensitivity of the TotalCharges choice

Variance inflation factors (VIF) show how much each feature is explained by the others; values above 10 are normally a concern.

In [49]:
def vif_table(frame):
    Z = (frame - frame.mean()) / frame.std()
    out = {}
    for c in Z.columns:
        yv = Z[c].values
        Xv = np.c_[np.ones(len(Z)), Z.drop(columns=c).values]
        beta = np.linalg.lstsq(Xv, yv, rcond=None)[0]
        r2 = 1 - ((yv - Xv @ beta) ** 2).sum() / ((yv - yv.mean()) ** 2).sum()
        out[c] = 1 / (1 - r2)
    return pd.Series(out, name="VIF").sort_values(ascending=False)

TotalCharges itself is fine. The high values for fiber optic and monthly charges are structural: the price of a plan is largely decided by the internet type, so the two move together. Both are real business drivers, so they are kept (the regularised model copes with this).

Sensitivity test. Does the treatment of TotalCharges matter? The same pipeline is rerun with (a) totals as reported, (b) totals that disagree with the expected bill by more than 50% replaced by tenure x monthly charges, and (c) the column dropped.

In [51]:
def quick_run(frame, drop_total=False, fix_total=False):
    d = frame.copy()
    if fix_total:
        ratio = d["TotalCharges"] / (d["tenure"] * d["MonthlyCharges"])
        bad = (d["tenure"] > 0) & ((ratio < 0.5) | (ratio > 1.5))
        d.loc[bad, "TotalCharges"] = (d["tenure"] * d["MonthlyCharges"])[bad]
    yy = (d["Churn"] == "Yes").astype(int)
    xa, xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(d.drop(columns="Churn"), yy, test_size=0.20, stratify=yy, random_state=SEED)
    ea, eb = encode(xa), encode(xb)
    imp_ = rf_imputer().fit(ea)
    def _imp(e):
        o = pd.DataFrame(imp_.transform(e), columns=e.columns, index=e.index)
        o["tenure"] = o["tenure"].round().clip(0, ea["tenure"].max())
        o["MonthlyCharges"] = o["MonthlyCharges"].clip(ea["MonthlyCharges"].min(), ea["MonthlyCharges"].max())
        m_ = e["TotalCharges"].isna()
        o.loc[m_, "TotalCharges"] = o.loc[m_, "tenure"] * o.loc[m_, "MonthlyCharges"]
        o["log_tenure"] = np.log1p(o["tenure"])
        return o.drop(columns="tenure")
    oa, ob = _imp(ea), _imp(eb)
    if drop_total:
        oa, ob = oa.drop(columns="TotalCharges"), ob.drop(columns="TotalCharges")
    sc_cols = [c for c in ["log_tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"] if c in oa.columns]
    s_ = StandardScaler().fit(oa[sc_cols])
    oa[sc_cols], ob[sc_cols] = s_.transform(oa[sc_cols]), s_.transform(ob[sc_cols])
    m = LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=3000).fit(oa, ya)
    pred, prob = m.predict(ob), m.predict_proba(ob)[:, 1]
    return {"Recall": recall_score(yb, pred), "Precision": precision_score(yb, pred),
            "F1": f1_score(yb, pred), "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(yb, prob)}

sens = pd.DataFrame({"(a) As reported": quick_run(df), "(b) Inconsistent totals corrected": quick_run(df, fix_total=True),
                     "(c) TotalCharges dropped": quick_run(df, drop_total=True)}).T
sens.map(lambda v: f"{v:.4f}")

3.12 Data leakage review

Risk How it was handled
Test data influencing preprocessing Split first; imputer and scaler fitted on the training set only
Target used to fill or build features Churn was never an input to the imputer or to any engineered feature
Features that contain the outcome No column records a cancellation date, reason or final bill; TotalCharges is a running total of past billing, not an outcome
Information shared between train and test rows Repeat entries removed before the split
Choosing settings on the test set Feature choices were made with cross-validation on the training set; the test set is used once for the final baseline scores

4. Model Building: Baseline Model

4.1 Metric of choice

A missed churner (false negative) costs the customer's remaining revenue. A wrongly flagged loyal customer (false positive) costs one retention offer. The first mistake is normally far more expensive than the second, so the model should be judged mainly on recall for the churn class: the share of real churners it catches. Precision and F1 are watched alongside it so the model cannot reach high recall by flagging everybody, and ROC-AUC / PR-AUC show how well it ranks customers regardless of the cut-off. Plain accuracy is not used for selection, because predicting "nobody churns" is already about 72% accurate.

A rough sizing of what is at stake, from the cleaned data:

4.2 Baseline model: logistic regression

Logistic regression is the baseline because it is simple, quick, and its coefficients can be read directly. Three versions are compared on the test set: a "predict the majority class" dummy, logistic regression without class weights, and logistic regression with balanced class weights.

In [53]:
def score_all(model, X_, y_, threshold=0.5):
    prob = model.predict_proba(X_)[:, 1]
    pred = (prob >= threshold).astype(int)
    return {"Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_, pred), "Precision": precision_score(y_, pred, zero_division=0),
            "Recall": recall_score(y_, pred), "F1": f1_score(y_, pred),
            "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_, prob), "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(y_, prob)}

dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy="prior").fit(X_train_s, y_train)
lr_plain = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000, random_state=SEED).fit(X_train_s, y_train)
lr_base = LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=3000, random_state=SEED).fit(X_train_s, y_train)

compare = pd.DataFrame({"Majority-class dummy": score_all(dummy, X_test_s, y_test),
                        "Logistic regression (no weights)": score_all(lr_plain, X_test_s, y_test),

What the model learned. Coefficients of the logistic regression, shown as odds ratios (the factor by which the odds of churn are multiplied when the feature goes up by one unit; for the standardised columns, one standard deviation). Above 1 raises churn risk, below 1 lowers it.

# how well does the ranking concentrate churners at the top?
rank = pd.DataFrame({"prob": prob_test, "churn": y_test.values}).sort_values("prob", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
rank["decile"] = pd.qcut(rank.index, 10, labels=range(1, 11))
gain = rank.groupby("decile", observed=True).agg(Customers=("churn", "size"), Churners=("churn", "sum"))
gain["Churn rate (%)"] = gain["Churners"] / gain["Customers"] * 100
gain["Cumulative % of churners caught"] = gain["Churners"].cumsum() / gain["Churners"].sum() * 100
gain["Lift"] = gain["Churn rate (%)"] / (y_test.mean() * 100)
display(gain)

4.4 Summary of the baseline

  • Balanced logistic regression on 23 prepared features. Test set (2,406 customers): recall 0.79, precision 0.58, F1 0.67, ROC-AUC 0.86.
  • Without class weights, recall is only 0.55. The ROC-AUC is the same, so the weights move the cut-off along one curve, they do not improve the ranking.
  • Train, test and 5-fold cross-validation scores agree to within about 0.01: no sign of over-fitting.
  • The strongest drivers match the EDA: fiber optic and DSL (against no internet), month-to-month contracts, electronic-check payment, short tenure, no tech support or online security.
  • The top 20% of customers by predicted risk contain about 51% of all churners; the top 40% contain about 80%.
  • Limits: a linear model cannot capture interactions, and about 42% of flagged customers are false alarms. The advanced models in the final submission must beat these figures, mainly on recall.
